sections.heading: Inside a solar cell, one level deeper: band gaps and passivation
bullets: A semiconductor's band gap is the energy toll for freeing an electron: photons below it pass through unused, and any photon energy above it is shed as heat. Silicon's ~1.1 electron-volt gap sits near the sweet spot for sunlight — but still caps a single-junction silicon cell around 29% efficiency

Real cells lose most of their remaining potential at surfaces: a freed electron that meets a dangling silicon bond or a metal contact 'recombines' and is wasted. Modern cell design is largely surface engineering — passivation layers that chemically calm those surfaces without blocking current flow

The acronyms are passivation strategies: PERC adds a passivating rear layer with tiny contact openings; TOPCon adds an ultra-thin tunnel oxide under a polysilicon layer, letting current tunnel through while keeping recombination-prone metal off the wafer; HJT wraps the wafer in amorphous silicon films

The industry's shift from p-type to n-type wafers (phosphorus-doped base instead of boron) removed the boron-oxygen defect that degraded cells under their first sunlight and raised the efficiency ceiling — TOPCon won the transition largely because it could be built on upgraded PERC production lines

sections.heading: From polysilicon to module: the five-stage value chain
bullets: Five stages stand between quartz and a rooftop: polysilicon (ultra-pure refined silicon) → ingots (melted and crystallized) → wafers (sawn slices thinner than a business card) → cells (junction, passivation, metal contacts) → modules (cells strung, laminated under glass, framed). Vertical integration means owning most or all of them

Each stage is its own industry with its own capacity cycle, and margin migrates to whichever stage is tightest: when polysilicon is short, refiners take the chain's profit while everyone downstream squeezes; in a glut, no stage earns. Integration is a hedge against being the squeezed stage

Wafer economics is a war on waste: sawing loses silicon as dust (kerf), so cutting wire gets finer and wafers thinner, while larger wafer formats spread handling cost over more watts. Cell economics obsesses over silver — the contact paste is the biggest non-silicon materials cost, driving copper-plating research

The module step looks mundane — glass, encapsulant, frame, junction box — but it sets field reliability: lamination quality decides whether moisture reaches the cells in year 20. It is also where differentiation lives: interconnection styles, glass-glass bifacial builds, and format choices all happen here

sections.heading: Tariffs, traceability, onshoring: trade policy as industry economics
bullets: Anti-dumping and countervailing duties (AD/CVD) are tariffs set per company, per country, calculated from investigations into below-cost selling and subsidies. Producers respond by moving assembly to third countries — which triggers new investigations chasing the supply chain there, a multi-round pursuit

Forced-labor traceability rules flip the burden of proof: imports are presumed non-compliant unless the importer documents every input back to the polysilicon's origin. Origin paperwork becomes part of the product — and suppliers who cannot produce it are excluded regardless of price

Onshoring math: a domestic factory runs at higher labor and energy cost, but earns tariff-free market access and often production incentives. The build-or-ship decision weighs the tariff-plus-freight burden against the domestic cost gap minus incentives — policy, not physics, sets the answer

The result is product segmentation by geography: manufacturers route different factories' output to different markets, launch region-specific product versions, and sometimes skip a market entirely when the tariff math fails. Reading a solar maker's factory map is reading its trade-policy strategy

sections.heading: Module reliability: why a 30-year warranty is an engineering claim
bullets: Modules degrade through named mechanisms: LID (light-induced degradation — boron-oxygen defects activated by first sun), LeTID (light and elevated temperature), PID (potential-induced — system voltage driving ions through the glass), plus cell microcracks, solder fatigue, and encapsulant browning

The warranty curve is a physics claim in legal form: a typical promise allows a small first-year drop then roughly 0.4% loss per year, guaranteeing ~87-90% of rated output at year 30. Project financiers price electricity on that curve, so beating or missing it is worth real money

Nobody waits 30 years to find out: accelerated testing compresses decades into chambers — damp heat (85°C at 85% humidity), thermal cycling from -40°C to +85°C, mechanical loading, hail impact — and independent labs run extended protocols beyond certification minimums to rank manufacturers publicly

The temperature coefficient — percent of output lost per degree above 25°C — quietly separates modules: panels routinely run 20-30°C above ambient, so a better coefficient delivers its advantage exactly where sunlight is strongest. Small spec differences compound into measurable annual energy

sections.heading: Bifacial modules and the energy-yield mindset
bullets: A bifacial module's rear face collects light reflected off the ground (albedo) plus diffuse sky light — a 5-20% energy bonus depending on the surface below: grass reflects little, sand more, white gravel or snow the most. The module's nameplate rating barely changes; its annual harvest does

The bifaciality factor — rear-side efficiency as a percentage of front-side — is set by cell architecture: passivation-based designs leave the rear naturally semi-transparent, and rear metallization coverage decides how much light gets through. A higher factor turns the same ground reflection into more energy

Bifacial gains stack with mounting choices: elevated racking and single-axis trackers expose more rear-side light than low fixed-tilt rows. This couples module choice to plant design — the same panel yields differently depending on the field built around it

The professional metric is energy yield — kilowatt-hours per kilowatt of nameplate per year — not wattage: two modules with identical ratings produce different annual energy once temperature behavior, bifacial gain, low-light response, and degradation are modeled. Buyers simulate; spec-sheet watts are the start, not the answer

sections.heading: Boom, bust, repeat: commodity cycles in manufacturing
bullets: Solar manufacturing overshoots structurally: capacity is added in giant increments on multi-year lead times against smoothly growing demand. Every producer expands during the boom, the new capacity lands together, and prices crash below cash cost — a cycle the industry has now run several times

In a price war, commodity pricing gravitates to the most efficient producer's cash cost — and factories keep running at a loss because stopping loses more: fixed costs continue, restarts are expensive, and market share is forfeited. Industry-wide losses can persist for years

Cycles end through exits and discipline: weaker producers fail or consolidate, and survivors attempt coordinated capacity restraint — inherently fragile, since every participant gains by quietly defecting while the others hold back. Watch actual capacity retirements, not announcements, for the real signal

The strategic escape is de-commoditization: attach differentiated, stickier products — storage systems, integrated energy solutions — to the same customer channel, or push technology transitions fast enough that your product is not interchangeable. A commodity maker's storage division is often its margin lifeboat

flashcards.q: What is a band gap, and why is silicon's nearly ideal for solar?
flashcards.a: The minimum photon energy needed to free an electron in a semiconductor. Photons below the gap pass through unused; energy above it is shed as heat. Silicon's ~1.1 eV gap balances those two losses well against the solar spectrum — though it still caps single-junction silicon cells at roughly 29% efficiency.

flashcards.q: What is recombination, and what does passivation do about it?
flashcards.a: Recombination is a freed electron falling back into place before it is collected — its energy wasted as heat. It happens mostly at surfaces and metal contacts, where the crystal ends in defects. Passivation layers chemically satisfy those surfaces to suppress recombination while still letting current out — the core trick behind every modern cell architecture.

flashcards.q: Distinguish PERC, TOPCon, and HJT in one line each.
flashcards.a: PERC: a passivating rear layer with small openings for contact — the former mainstream. TOPCon: an ultra-thin tunnel oxide plus polysilicon layer that passes current while keeping recombination-prone contacts off the wafer — today's mainstream, partly because PERC lines upgrade to it. HJT: the wafer sandwiched in amorphous silicon films — excellent passivation, but a different production line entirely.

flashcards.q: Why did the industry switch from p-type to n-type wafers?
flashcards.a: P-type wafers are boron-doped, and boron pairs with trace oxygen to form defects activated by the first sunlight exposure — light-induced degradation. N-type (phosphorus-doped) wafers avoid that defect and support higher efficiency ceilings. TOPCon rode the transition to mainstream because it reused much of the existing production base.

flashcards.q: Name the five stages of the solar value chain and where the profit sits.
flashcards.a: Polysilicon → ingot → wafer → cell → module. Each stage has its own capacity cycle, and the chain's margin migrates to whichever stage is scarcest — a polysilicon shortage lets refiners take nearly all the profit while downstream stages squeeze. Vertical integration is a hedge against being the squeezed stage.

flashcards.q: What are kerf loss and the silver problem in solar cost engineering?
flashcards.a: Kerf is silicon lost as sawdust when ingots are cut into wafers — attacked with finer cutting wire and thinner wafers. Silver paste forms the cell's electrical contacts and is the biggest non-silicon materials cost, which is why silver-reduction and copper-plating research matter at industry consumption scale.

flashcards.q: How do AD/CVD tariffs work, and how do manufacturers respond?
flashcards.a: Anti-dumping and countervailing duties are set per company and per country after investigations into below-cost selling and subsidies. Producers relocate assembly to unaffected countries; investigations then follow the supply chain there. The multi-round chase reshapes factory maps — trade policy, not logistics, decides where solar factories get built.

flashcards.q: What do forced-labor traceability rules change for a module seller?
flashcards.a: They reverse the burden of proof: shipments are presumed non-compliant unless the importer documents every input's origin back to the polysilicon. Origin documentation becomes part of the product itself — a supplier who cannot produce the paperwork is excluded from the market regardless of price or performance.

LID (light-induced degradation): boron-oxygen defects in p-type wafers activate under first sunlight, permanently trimming output — a key driver of the n-type transition. PID (potential-induced degradation): the voltage difference between cells and the grounded frame drives ions through the glass and degrades the cell — countered by cell design, encapsulant choice, and system grounding.

flashcards.q: How does anyone verify a 30-year module warranty without waiting 30 years?
flashcards.a: Accelerated stress testing: damp heat (85°C at 85% humidity), hundreds of thermal cycles between -40°C and +85°C, mechanical loading, and hail impact compress decades of stress into weeks. Certification sets the minimums; independent labs run extended protocols and publish rankings that buyers and financiers treat as the reliability scoreboard.

flashcards.q: What determines how much extra energy a bifacial module harvests?
flashcards.a: The ground's reflectivity (albedo — grass low, sand more, white gravel or snow highest), the module's bifaciality factor (rear efficiency as a share of front), and mounting that exposes the rear side — elevation and trackers help. Gains run roughly 5-20% in annual energy with almost no change in nameplate watts.

flashcards.q: Why do solar manufacturers lose money for years yet keep running — and how do cycles end?
flashcards.a: Capacity arrives in giant, slow-to-build increments, so booms overshoot and prices fall to the best producer's cash cost. Stopping loses more than running — fixed costs continue, restarts cost, share is forfeited — so losses persist. Cycles end through exits, consolidation, and fragile capacity discipline; firms escape by de-commoditizing into storage and integrated products.
